cim: Amini Releases Soma, an Open Artificial Intelligence (AI) Model to Take Nations from Analogue to AI-Ready
cim_eredeti: Amini Releases Soma, an Open Artificial Intelligence (AI) Model to Take Nations from Analogue to AI-Ready
szoveg_eredeti:
Amini released Soma-1X Lite, a compact, open-weight AI model that converts paper records into structured, machine-readable data. Small enough to run on a single GPU within a government’s sovereign infrastructure, Soma shows that countries of the Global South can build world-class AI for their own context, on their own terms. The AI model is available today on Hugging Face.

The biggest leapfrog opportunity of the AI age

Across the Global South, most knowledge remains offline. It sits on paper: cabinet papers, land registries, civil registries, geological surveys, and handwritten ledgers in languages no AI benchmark was designed to test. Because AI learns from what it can read, those countries are largely absent from the systems now shaping the global economy.

Amini sees in that gap an opportunity. Countries that have never fully digitised do not need to move from analogue to digital and then, a decade later, from digital to AI. They can go straight from analogue to AI-ready. That takes tools that handle difficult documents at national scale and run on infrastructure a country controls. Soma was designed around those requirements:

“Constraint has always been our superpower,” said Kate Kallot, founder and CEO of Amini. “We did not ask how big we could build. We asked how small we could build and still stand among the best in the world.”

“This is the biggest leapfrog opportunity of the AI age, and the biggest opportunity for inclusion,” Kallot added. “Inclusion is not a seat at a table someone else built. It is our languages, our stories, our culture and our knowledge systems, read correctly and kept at home.”

Soma’s story began in Barbados. Through R.O.A.D. (Reclaiming Our Atlantic Destiny) (https://Road.bb/), the Government of Barbados is preserving and digitising one of the world’s most extensive archives documenting the history of Atlantic slave societies: millions of pages, many handwritten, fragile and centuries old. Working on these records, alongside cabinet papers and other government archives, shaped how Soma was built. Faded ink, handwritten annotations, complex tables and damaged pages became the problems the model was trained and tested to solve.

Over the past year, Soma has processed millions of government records in private, sovereign environments. The work has since extended to Botswana, where Amini is digitizing geological maps and mineral resource records still on paper, with the Central African Republic to follow.

“These records are not simply collections of names, dates and events; they hold the traces of human lives. Some people are named, and others appear only in fragments in the official record. Making these materials searchable is important, but it is part of the deeper work of restoring memory, dignity and humanity, enabling Barbadians and the wider diaspora to find themselves in the record, reconnect families and communities, and reclaim histories thought to be long lost. Our partnership with Amini demonstrates what becomes possible when technology is designed in service of the archive, and with people first.” Chereda Grannum, Programme Manager, ROAD

Soma is released with open weights, so any government, archive, university or developer can run it privately and build on it. It builds on open-source research, and Amini is returning its work to that community.

Its origins span regions: an African company, the archives of a Caribbean nation, the geological records of Botswana and ten African languages. Amini sees this as a model for how Global South countries can reduce dependence on a handful of frontier providers: by pooling knowledge, sharing models and solving common challenges together.

“The Global South has as much to teach AI as it has to gain from it. We chose Amini because they share that conviction. Together, we’ve turned Cabinet papers and centuries of Barbadian history into intelligence our citizens and public servants use every day. Soma-1X Lite shows we can build world-class AI on our own terms. And when we build for the Global South, we build for most of humanity.” – Senator the Hon. Jonathan Reid, Minister of Innovation, Industry, Science and Technology of Barbados

Amini is releasing Soma-1X Lite’s model weights, inference instructions, and evaluation code, enabling researchers and developers to reproduce its results, build upon the model, and adapt it to their own needs.

The next release will extend Soma to more underrepresented languages and scripts, historical and handwritten archives, and complex records such as maps, forms and registries. Through continued research, and real world feedback from its government deployments, Amini aims to make document intelligence more capable, accessible, and relevant to institutions worldwide.
